title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-283-790-001
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-283-790-001
Issues
Whether Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence he is entitled to
⮚
temporary total disability (TTD) benefits from March 13, 2025 to February 11,
2026.
Whether Respondents proved by a preponderance of the evidence Claimant is
⮚
responsible for his termination from employment and thus not entitled to TTD.
Whether Claimant is entitled to an award of disfigurement benefits.
⮚
Stipulations
At hearing, the ALJ accepted the following stipulations of the parties:
1. Claimant was placed at maximum medical improvement (MMI) by Dr. Scott
Primack on February 11, 2026.
2. The contract term that Claimant was playing under at the time of injury was for
the 2024/2025 season where he earned $1,055,000. His average weekly wage
(AWW) is $20,288.
3. Respondent paid salary continuation from the date of injury (7/31/2024) to March
12, 2025.
4. The claimed wage loss period is from March 13, 2025 to February 11, 2026.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant is 31 years old. Claimant was employed by Employer, a National
Football League Team (NFL) team, as a professional football player.
1

2. On July 31, 2024, Claimant suffered an admitted industrial injury while
participating in team practice. Claimant sustained a right ankle Maisonneuve
fracture and dislocation.
3. At the time of the industrial injury Claimant was under contract with Employer for
one football season. Claimant’s NFL Player Contract, executed on March 6,
2024, provided that the contract term covered one football season, beginning on
the date of execution and ending the last day of the 2024 League Year, unless
extended or renewed.
4. As a result of the industrial injury, Employer placed Claimant on injured reserve
on August 1, 2024. The injury was classified by Employer as “major,” with an
estimated time loss of six to nine months from the date of injury.
5. Claimant underwent multiple surgeries for the industrial injury performed by
authorized treating physician (ATP) Joshua Metzl, MD, including a right ankle
arthroscopic debridement with syndesmotic open reduction and internal fixation
repair and deltoid ligament repair on August 7, 2024, and hardware removals on
September 30, 2024 and October 24, 2024. Claimant attended multiple post-
operative physical therapy sessions.
6. On January 13, 2025, Dr. Metzl conducted Claimant’s end of season physical for
Employer. On examination, Dr. Metzl noted mild ankle swelling with no pain
through ankle range of motion. Dr. Metzl determined that Claimant failed the
physical exam, noting that Claimant would have to wait for clearance for another
eight weeks as physical therapy progressed. Claimant testified that he did not
return to Dr. Metzel in eight weeks because his contract with Employer
subsequently ended and he thus did not have access to see Dr. Metzel at that
time.
7. Claimant continued physical therapy and rehabilitation with Employer’s provider,
attending sessions 5 days/week every week until March 11, 2025. Claimant
ceased attending physical therapy and rehabilitation with Employer’s provider
because he became a free agent upon expiration of his contract. The team’s
2

provider noted, “[Claimant] reported today that he would be foregoing the last two
days of rehab as he will become a free agent after Wednesday. [Claimant] and I
discussed continued therapy and we have help set him up with NextLevel
Physical Therapy where he will continue his rehab on Thursday 3/13/25.” [RHE
B, p. 67].
8. Claimant did not play the entire 2024 football season due to his industrial injury.
Employer paid Claimant salary continuation through March 12, 2025, as provided
under Claimant’s contract. Claimant’s contract with Employer ended by its own
terms on March 12, 2025 at the conclusion of the 2024 football season.
9. On March 13, 2025, Claimant presented to Next Level Physical Therapy (Next
Level) for continued care of his right ankle injury. The physical therapist noted
that Claimant was advancing in strength, running, jumping and light field work,
but continued to have limitations with dorsiflexion, swelling, stiffness, joint
mobility restriction and altered movement. The physical therapist remarked that
Claimant would “need focused intervention to aide in his ability to return to
professional football.” CHE 4, p. 9. Claimant was to attend physical therapy 4
days/week for 12 weeks.
10. Claimant continued to attend physical therapy at NextLevel, as well as at
UCHealth Physical Therapy and Rehabilitation Clinic. On September 22 and
October 6, 2025, the physical therapist noted that Claimant presented with
impaired ankle range of motion, swelling, pain and mobility. It was noted that
physical therapy was required for Claimant to address these impairments and to
safely return to playing professional football.
11. In October 2025, despite not being cleared to return to play football or released
from care, Claimant participated in a tryout for Employer in hopes of getting re-
signed by the team and returning to play as an offensive lineman. Claimant
executed Employer’s Release and Waiver on October 13, 2025 representing, in
part, “…that I am in good health and sound physical condition, and that I have no
physical defects, conditions or injuries, latent or patent that would endanger my
3

health or that may be aggravated or exacerbated by the tryout…” [RHE F, p.
329].
12. Claimant credibly testified at hearing. Claimant testified that he signed the waiver
and attended the tryout because, prior to the tryout, he felt good and believed
that he was able to play. However, during the tryout, he experienced continued
issues with ankle range of motion and load bearing and realized that he was
unable to participate in professional football activities at that time.
13. Respondent did not offer Claimant a contract after the tryout.
14. On January 6, 2026, Claimant returned to Dr. Metzl on the referral of his primary
care physician at UC Health. Dr. Metzl noted that Claimant overall had steady
improvement since his surgeries and continued to train for a potential return to
the NFL. Claimant reported experiencing daily pain and stiffness in his ankle. Dr.
Metzl noted radiographic signs of anterior impingement with posttraumatic ankle
arthrosis. Dr. Metzl wrote, “We discussed that he will continue training and if the
pain is persistent he would be a good candidate for arthroscopy with anterior
decompression. He expressed understanding and will see me back on a [sic] as
needed basis.” [CHE 7, p. 41].
15. On February 11, 2026, Scott Primack, DO, conducted an Independent Medical
Examination (IME) at request of Respondent. Claimant reported persistent ankle
stiffness. Dr. Primack placed Claimant at MMI as of the date of his IME and
assigned a 12% lower extremity impairment rating. Dr. Primack remarked,
“[Claimant] certainly can perform the essential functions of a job in many
positions; however, it is fairly obvious that he would not be able to adequately
perform the essential functions of the job as an offensive lineman in the National
Football League given his residual stiffness.” [CHE 8, p. 46].
16. Dr. Primack credibly testified at hearing on behalf of Respondents. Dr. Primack
testified as a Level II accredited expert in physical medicine and rehabilitation
and occupational medicine. Dr. Primack testified consistent with his IME report.
He testified that, at the time of his IME, he was unaware that Claimant had
4

participated in team tryouts in October 2025; however, such knowledge did not
change any of his opinions.
17. Claimant and Employer entered multiple Practice Player and NFL Player
contracts over the course of approximately six football seasons. Employer has a
history of offering new contracts to Claimant despite terminating his contracts for
purported unsatisfactory skill or performance. On September 1, 2019, Employer
terminated Claimant’s 2019-2021 contract citing the following reason: “In the
judgment of the Club, your skill or performance has been unsatisfactory as
compared with that of other players competing for positions on the Club’s roster.”
[RHE F, p.197]. Employer cited the same reason when terminating Claimant’s
2020-2021 contract on September 6, 2020, Claimant’s 2021-2022 contract on
September 1, 2021, Claimant’s 2022-2023 contract on August 31, 2022,
Claimant’s 2022-2023 contract on December 7, 2022, and Claimant’s 2023-2024
contract on August 29, 2023.
18. Claimant testified that when he signed his 2024 contract, his plan at the
expiration of the contract was to continue playing in the NFL. Claimant testified
he would have liked to continue playing for Employer, but understood there was
no guarantee, as he was set to become an unrestricted free agent at the
expiration of his 2024 contract. Claimant testified that he failed Employer’s end of
season physical, which meant he was neither cleared to play nor able to play at
the time. Claimant explained that his position as an offensive lineman required,
among other things, bracing, impact, pushing, and running. Claimant testified that
the industrial injury resulted in decreased stability, strength, and range of motion
that affected his ability to effectively run, bend, and produce explosive
movements as required of his position. Claimant testified that, at the time his
2024 contract expired, he was unable to perform his offensive lineman duties due
to the industrial injury but continued with treatment in hopes of continuing to play
and re-signing with Employer.
5

19. Respondent’s Vice President of Football Administration, Rich Hurtado, credibly
testified at hearing on behalf of Employer. Mr. Hurtado’s role involves negotiating
player contracts, managing the club’s salary cap, and strategic planning with the
general manager regarding player acquisition and roster construction. Mr.
Hurtado explained that the employment relationship between Employer and the
players is governed by a collective bargaining agreement. Mr. Hurtado engaged
in contract negotiations with Claimant’s agent on multiple contracts, including
Claimant’s 2024-2025 contract. Mr. Hurtado testified that Claimant’s agent
negotiated a one-year term, as Claimant was set to become an unrestricted free
agent at the end of the 2024-2025 football season. Mr. Hurtado explained that an
unrestricted free agent is where the team would have, “no right to keep the player
unless he’s really, really talented and we can place what’s called a franchiser
transition tag.” [Hr. Tr. p. 49, l. 15-18]. Mr. Hurtado testified that, at the time of
Claimant’s 2024 contract negotiations, the team did not intend to keep Claimant
as a franchise player.
20. Mr. further Hurtado testified that Claimant’s 2024 contract expired and the team
decided not to re-sign Claimant. Mr. Hurtado testified that he was involved in
Employer’s decision not to offer Claimant a new contract at the end of the 2024
football season. Mr. Hurtado acknowledged that a player’s availability and health
are factors in remaining competitive but testified that Claimant’s industrial injury
was not the reason Employer did not re-sign Claimant. Mr. Hurtado testified that,
at the time, the team already had 12 good lineman and decided to look towards
the draft and college free agency to further enhance the offensive line. Mr.
Hurtado testified that Claimant was not competitive with the other players the
team was considering for the offensive lineman positions and that other players
were better alternatives.
21. Claimant has not returned to playing professional football. Claimant has not
earned any wages since March 13, 2025.
6

22. Claimant proved it is more probably true than not he is entitled to TTD benefits
March 13, 2025 to February 11, 2026. The July 31, 2024 industrial injury to
caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts. As a result of the
disability, Claimant left work and sustained wage loss.
23. Respondents failed to prove it is more probably true than not Claimant was
responsible for the termination of employment. The termination of employment
was the result of the natural expiration of the fixed term of Claimant’s 2024
contract. Claimant intended to continue working as an offensive lineman in the
NFL upon expiration of the fixed term of the contract.
24. The ALJ observed Claimant’s right ankle at hearing and viewed photographs of
Claimant’s right ankle contained in Claimant’s Exhibit 12. As a result of his July
31, 2024 industrial injury, Claimant has a visible disfigurement consisting of the
following:
(1) A scar on Claimant’s inner right ankle measuring approximately 2.5 inches
in length and .5 inches in width. The scar is significantly darker in color than
the surrounding skin and textured. Suture scars are perceptible along the
length of the scar.
(2) A scar on Claimant’s inner right ankle measuring approximately 1 inch in
length and width. The scar is significantly darker in color than the surrounding
skin and textured. Suture scars perceptible along the length of the scar.
(3) A scar on the front of Claimant’s right ankle. The scar measures
approximately .5 inches in length and width and is darker in color than the
surrounding skin with minimal texture.
(4) A scar on Claimant’s outer right ankle measuring approximately 3 inches
in length and 1.25 inches in width. The scar is significantly darker in color
than the surrounding skin and textured, with suture scars perceptible along
the length of the scar.
7

25. Claimant has sustained a serious permanent disfigurement to areas of the body
normally expos and shall be awarded $3,750.00.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S. is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
8

Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors, Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
TTD Benefits
D. To prove entitlement to TTD benefits, a claimant must prove that the industrial
injury caused a disability lasting more than three work shifts, he left work as a
result of the disability, and the disability resulted in an actual wage loss. See §§8-
42-(1)(g) & 8-42-105(4), C.R.S.; Anderson v. Longmont Toyota, 102 P.3d 323
(Colo. 2004); City of Colorado Springs v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 954 P.2d
637 (Colo. App. 1997). Section 8-42-103(1)(a), C.R.S. requires the claimant to
establish a causal connection between a work-related injury and a subsequent
wage loss in order to obtain TTD benefits. The term “disability” connotes two
elements: (1) medical incapacity evidenced by loss or restriction of bodily
function; and (2) impairment of wage earning capacity as demonstrated by
claimant's inability to resume his or her prior work. Culver v. Ace Electric, 971
P.2d 641, 649 (Colo. 1999). The impairment of earning capacity element of
disability may be evidenced by a complete inability to work or by restrictions
which impair the claimant's ability effectively and properly to perform his or her
regular employment. Ortiz v. Charles J. Murphy & Co., 964 P.2d 595, 597 (Colo.
App. 1998). Because there is no requirement that a claimant must produce
evidence of medical restrictions, a claimant’s testimony alone is sufficient to
demonstrate a disability. Lymburn v. Symbios Logic, 952 P.2d 831, 833 (Colo.
App. 1997).
9

E. TTD benefits shall continue until the first occurrence of any of the following: (1)
the employee reaches MMI; (2) the employee returns to regular or modified
employment; (3) the attending physician gives the employee a written release to
return to regular employment; or (4) the attending physician gives the employee
a written release to return to modified employment, the employment is offered in
writing and the employee fails to begin the employment. §8-42-105(3)(a)-(d),
C.R.S.; see Chavez v. Costco Wholesale, Inc., WC 5-096-055-003 (ICAO, Feb.
4, 2022) (noting that, where TTD benefits had not commenced, they could not be
terminated based on the ATP’s MMI determination).
F. As found, Claimant proved it is more probable than not he is entitled to TTD
benefits from March 13, 2025 to February 11, 2026. The July 31, 2024 industrial
injury to Claimant’s right ankle caused disability both in the form of loss and
restriction of Claimant’s bodily function and impairment of his wage earning
capacity. As credibly and persuasively testified to by Claimant and documented
in the medical records, the industrial injury caused deficits in range of motion and
persistent stiffness, which impaired his ability to effectively and properly perform
as an offensive lineman. As a result of the industrial injury, Claimant was placed
on injured reserve and was unable to play the entire 2024 season. Subsequent to
the expiration of his contract, Claimant remained unable to adequately perform
his duties as an offensive lineman as a result of the effects of the industrial injury.
Claimant continued treatment for the industrial injury yet was not cleared by any
physician to return to his regular work activities as an offensive lineman. The
industrial injury impaired Claimant’s wage earning capacity as demonstrated by
claimant's inability to resume his prior work, resulting in actual wage loss for
Claimant. Claimant therefore is entitled to TTD benefits from March 13, 2025 to
February 11, 2026, the date of MMI.
Responsibility for Termination
G. Under the termination statutes in §§8-42-105(4) & 8-42-103(1)(g) C.R.S. a
claimant who is responsible for his or her termination from regular or modified
10

employment is not entitled to TTD benefits absent a worsening of condition that
reestablishes the causal connection between the industrial injury and wage loss.
Gilmore v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 187 P.3d 1129, 1131 (Colo. App. 2008).
The termination statutes provide that, in cases where an employee is responsible
for her termination, the resulting wage loss is not attributable to the industrial
injury. In re of Davis, WC 4-631-681 (ICAO, Apr. 24, 2006). A claimant does not
act “volitionally” or exercise control over the circumstances leading to her
termination if the effects of the injury prevent her from performing her assigned
duties and cause the termination. In re of Eskridge, WC 4-651-260 (ICAO, Apr.
21, 2006). Therefore, to establish that Claimant was responsible for their
termination, respondents must demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence
that the claimant committed a volitional act or exercised some control over their
termination under the totality of the circumstances. See Padilla v. Digital
Equipment, 902 P.2d 414, 416 (Colo. App. 1994). An employee is thus
“responsible” if they precipitated the employment termination by a volitional act
that they would reasonably expect to cause the loss of employment. Patchek v.
Dep’t of Public Safety, WC 4-432-301 (ICAO, Sept. 27, 2001).
H. Respondents acknowledge that Claimant’s employment ended because his
contract expired by its own terms at the conclusion of the football season.
Respondents argue, however, that by voluntarily entering a negotiated fixed term
contract, Claimant exercised a degree of control over the duration of his
employment and the circumstances under which his employment would end, and
thus is responsible for the termination of employment. The ALJ disagrees.
I. The concept of “fault” as it is used in the unemployment insurance context is
instructive for purposes of the termination statutes. See Kaufman v. Noffsinger
Manufacturing, W.C. No. 4-608-836 (April 18, 2005). The Court of Appeals has
previously held in unemployment insurance cases that the mere fact parties
agreed and understood employment would end at the expiration of a fixed term is
not a basis for denying unemployment insurance benefits. In re Interrogatories by
11

Indus. Comm'n, 496 P.2d 1064 (Colo. App. 1972); Intermountain Jewish News,
Inc. v. Indus. Comm'n, 564 P.2d 132 (Colo. App. 1977). Thus, when the
separation from employment occurs solely as a result of the expiration of an
agreed upon fixed term, the claimant is not deemed at fault merely because he
agreed to the fixed term of employment.
J. The Panel has previously addressed Respondents’ argument in the context of
seasonal employment in Judd v. Antarctic Support Svcs., WC 4-457-362 (ICAO
June 2, 2003). In Judd, the claimant was employed on a seasonal basis and
entered into a series of seven-month contracts with the employer. The ALJ
awarded the claimant TTD benefits for a period of time after the expiration of his
last contract. The respondents argued that the claimant was responsible for
termination of employment because he engaged in a volitional act leading to his
unemployment by voluntarily entering a fixed term contract. The Panel agreed
with the ALJ that, “the respondents’ proposed interpretation of the word
responsible ‘would bring about quite unreasonable, and unjust, results.” Id. The
Panel concluded that the loss of seasonal employment does not automatically
disqualify a claimant from receiving subsequent temporary disability benefits.
Rather, the question of whether the claimant's post-termination wage loss was
caused by the injury was one of fact for determination by the ALJ. Id. The Panel
cited City of Aurora v. Dortch, 799 P.2d 461 (Colo. App. 1990), where the court
concluded that a claimant's seasonal employment, which would have expired in
the month following her injury regardless of disability, did not preclude an award
of TTD benefits. The court emphasized that the evidence did not establish the
wage loss was either voluntary or due solely to the fact that her seasonal
employment would have expired. Id. at 462-63. The Panel in Judd stated,
Inherent in the Dortch decision is the court’s recognition
that seasonal employment is a common fact of economic life, and that the
conclusion of a particular period of seasonal employment should not
automatically be viewed as the permanent end to the employment
12

relationship or evidence of the claimant's “voluntary” decision to become
unemployed. Indeed, in many cases the end of seasonal employment is
best viewed as resulting from the unavailability of further work, an economic
factor for which the claimant is not at “fault.” In our opinion, it would be
contrary to the underlying purpose of the statutory scheme to hold, as a
matter of law, that termination of employment resulting from the conclusion
of a contract for seasonal work automatically disqualifies the claimant from
receiving subsequent TTD benefits. Cf. J.D. Lunsford v. Sawatsky, 780 P.2d
76 (Colo. App. 1989) (if claimant loses job because of economic factors and
is not at fault for the termination, claimant is entitled to TTD benefits). The
fact that the claimant knows the seasonal employment will end at a fixed
point in time does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that he is
responsible for the termination. City of Aurora v. Dortch, supra.
Judd v. Antarctic Support Svcs, supra.
K. While Claimant’s employment was not seasonal in the same exact sense, the
reasoning applies with respect to employment for an agreed upon fixed term. The
courts have also recognized that the result might be different if the ALJ were to
find the claimant selected a fixed period of seasonal employment with the intent
of remaining unemployed throughout a portion of the year, or permanently. See
El Paso County Department of Social Services v. Donn, 865 P.2d 877 (Colo.
App. 1986); Judd v. Antarctic Support Svcs, supra. The ALJ has made no such
finding in Claimant’s case. Claimant credibly and persuasively testified that, when
he signed his 2024 contract, his plan at the expiration of the contract was to
continue playing in the NFL and that he would have liked to continue playing for
Employer. As credibly and persuasively testified to by Claimant and documented
by providers, Claimant underwent extensive rehabilitation and training with the
intention of continuing to play NFL football. Despite not receiving physician
clearance, Claimant even participated in tryouts for Employer in October 2025 in
hopes of continuing his employment with the NFL. The evidence demonstrates
13

Claimant intended to continue working as an NFL player when he agreed to, and
upon the expiration of, his fixed term contract.
L. Claimant and Employer entered into multiple contracts over the course of six
seasons, with Employer citing unsatisfactory skill or performance as compared
with other players as the reason for termination of the contracts. Mr. Hurtado
testified that Employer’s decision not to offer Claimant a new contract in 2025
was based on Claimant’s performance compared to other players and not
Claimant’s industrial injury. While there was no guarantee Employer would offer
Claimant a new contract for the 2025 season upon the expiration of his 2024
contract, the evidence clearly demonstrates that the effects of the industrial injury
impaired Claimant’s ability to participate in professional football activities and
adequately perform his regular job duties, thus impairing his wage earning
capacity. As a result of the industrial injury, Claimant was unable to play the
entire 2024 season. He remained unable to play at the expiration of his contract
and no evidence was offered demonstrating Claimant was subsequently cleared
to play. Even when Claimant attempted to play during tryouts in October 2025,
he experienced continuing right ankle issues which impaired his ability to
adequately participate in professional football activities. Dr. Primack credibly
opined that, due to the residual effects of the industrial injury, it is “obvious”
Claimant would not be able to adequately perform the essential functions of the
job as an offensive lineman in the NFL.
M. In light of the totality of the circumstances of this case, the fact that Claimant’s
employment ended at the expiration of an agreed upon fixed term does not
render Claimant responsible for the termination of the employment and the
resulting wage loss.
Disfigurement
N. Section 8-42-108(1), C.R.S. provides that a claimant is entitled to additional
compensation if he is “seriously, permanently disfigured about the head, face, or
parts of the body normally exposed to public view.”
14

O. As found, Claimant sustained a serious permanent disfigurement to areas of the
body normally exposed to public view. Respondents shall pay Claimant
$3.750.00 for his disfigurement.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Claimant proved by a preponderance of the evidence that he is entitled to TTD
benefits from March 13, 2025, through February 11, 2026.
2. Respondents failed to prove by a preponderance of the evidence Claimant is
responsible for his termination from employment.
3. Respondents shall pay Claimant TTD benefits from March 13, 2025 to February
11, 2026.
4. Respondents shall pay Claimant $3,750.00 for his disfigurement.
5. Respondents shall pay statutory interest at a rate of 8% per annum on
compensation benefits not paid when due.
6. All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on the certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the ALJ's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20), days after mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you
mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
file your Petition to Review electronically by emailing the Petition to Review to the
following email address: oac-ptr@state.co.us. If the Petition to Review is emailed to the
aforementioned email address, the Petition to Review is deemed filed in Denver
pursuant to OACRP 27 and Section 8-43-301, C.R.S. If the Petition to Review is filed
15

by email to the proper email address, it does not need to be mailed to the Denver Office
of Administrative Courts. For further information regarding procedures to follow when
filing a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to review
form at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.
Dated: May 7, 2026
Kara R. Cayce
Administrative Law Judge
16
